source.title: Assessment of parasympathetic reactivation after exercise

paper.citation: Goldberger, J. J., Le, F. K., Lahiri, M., Kannankeril, P. J., Ng, J., & Kadish, A. H. (2006). Assessment of parasympathetic reactivation after exercise. American Journal of Physiology-Heart and Circulatory Physiology, 290(6), H2446–H2452. https://doi.org/10.1152/ajpheart.01118.2005
paper.abstract: Can RMS residual and successive-difference HRV measured immediately after exercise index parasympathetic reactivation against pharmacologic blockade? Ten healthy adults (five women; 33 ± 5 years) and 12 adults with coronary artery disease (two women; 61 ± 10 years). Laboratory cycling with 5-minute seated ECG recovery, tested with and without atropine. Clinical adult physiology context, not athlete-readiness validation. Within-person two-session exercise comparison using atropine 0.04 mg/kg as parasympathetic blockade. RMS residual, SD, and MSSD were calculated on successive 15-, 30-, and 60-second segments. The second session was not randomized because the first calibrated exercise intensity.
paper.tldr: This study informs what short-term postexercise HRV measures represent when heart rate is nonstationary. Thirty-second RMS and MSSD were related to the atropine-derived parasympathetic effect (R² = 0.47 and 0.56; both p < 0.0001). Interpretation should remain within the reviewed population, design, and applicability limits.
paper.methods: Within-person two-session exercise comparison using atropine 0.04 mg/kg as parasympathetic blockade. RMS residual, SD, and MSSD were calculated on successive 15-, 30-, and 60-second segments. The second session was not randomized because the first calibrated exercise intensity.
paper.findings: Thirty-second RMS and MSSD were related to the atropine-derived parasympathetic effect (R² = 0.47 and 0.56; both p < 0.0001). RMS remained approximately 1.7–2.1 ms across recovery under blockade, while unblocked RMS and MSSD rose over the first minute. Segment duration materially changed RMS values, supporting a fixed analysis window rather than interchangeable HRV epochs.
paper.limitations: Session order was not randomized, atropine administration was unblinded, and groups differed in age and exercise intensity. Small clinical samples limit population-specific precision. Validation against acute pharmacologic blockade does not establish day-to-day athlete monitoring reliability, sensitivity, or actionable thresholds. Standard frequency-domain HRV assumptions are problematic during nonstationary recovery.
paper.practicalImplications: If postexercise HRV is used, standardize posture, exercise dose, recovery timing, artifact handling, and epoch length. Do not treat a short-term recovery metric validated against atropine as automatically validated for readiness or training prescription in collegiate American football.
paper.athleteDev: For athlete-development decisions, use this evidence only within the reviewed population and context. If postexercise HRV is used, standardize posture, exercise dose, recovery timing, artifact handling, and epoch length. Do not treat a short-term recovery metric validated against atropine as automatically validated for readiness or training prescription in collegiate American football. Do not treat the study as a universal development pathway or benchmark.
paper.rtp: This study did not directly evaluate rehabilitation or return to sport. It provides no standalone clearance criterion, reinjury threshold, or validated return-to-play progression.
